story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I'm Ryan, I'm building Higherlevel (https://higherlevel.to) so product teams have one place to define and review software changes.

Over the last couple of years, I've been increasingly delegating software implementation to AI coding agents.

However, because it became easier and faster to ship complexity, I realised that it still takes me quite some time to even understand what the software is doing, why it is doing that, or review the changes.

I also don't do traditional code reviews anymore, it's mostly automated but I still want to review the final outcome of the changes (rather than its implementation).

I regularly work on complex B2B applications where a single feature can involve dozen of business rules, edge cases and interactions with existing functionality.

I found myself spending more and more time discovering and explaining requirements to agents, reviewing their output, asking for evdience and trying to establish whether we actually agreed on what correct behaviour looked like.

So I built Higherlevel. The idea is to bring product specifications and proof of work into a single collaborative workspace.

You can: - describe the current behaviour, known limitations and expected changes - define business rules, acceptance scenarios using Given/When/Then - demand evidence in the form of a screenshot, a video, etc - comment directly on the spec, on a specific area of the image or a timestamp of the video - discuss changes, track revisions and approve results with your team

I've written extensively about why I believe in specification driven development (and what it means to me) here https://higherlevel.to/blog/introducing-higherlevel

Higherlevel is currently in beta and built with Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, and PostgreSQL.

story_text.value:
As AI writes more and more of the code, it's quite important to maintain sufficient skill and knowledge to even review or judge AI's output.

Here is a little project I whipped up - I personally found deliberate practice quite useful. It focusses on non-coding skills (as I think LOC production is basically solved by AI, IMO). Rather I start with two tracks: general technical fluency (CS / systems / practical fundamentals), and system design.

And yes it was built primarily with help of AI tooling.

Would love to get some feedback - in particular, do others feel the same way about skill atrophy risk on-the-job nowadays, and whether this tool is helpful potentially or not. What else do folks do instead, if anything.

story_text.value:
I work with different AI coding tools, including codex, Claude,, Opencode, cursor, and others. Also, I work on several projects under different folders.

This makes managing skills, AGENTS.md files, MCPs so hard. I'm not sure what is installed where. Also, agents create memory files nowadays with instructions that I find misleading, so i wanna read and edit these memory files occasionally.

Thats why I created a tool with proper UI to manage all of these.

Opensource and local, check it out at: https://github.com/mjalalimanesh/skillhub-local

story_text.value:
I have been working on Rashomon, an open-source execution recorder for AI coding agents.

The basic idea is that the agent transcript is not ground truth. Rashomon keeps its own record of what happened and compares it against the agent’s account.

For Claude Code, it records things like:

* shell commands, exit codes, and whether they may have written files * tool calls and outcomes * test commands and their outcomes * subagent lifecycle and ordering * timestamps and parent/child relationships * keyed digests of command/tool inputs and working directories

It builds a timeline from these events. It does not store prompts, responses, file contents, or tool output.

For example, it now detects patterns like:

`test fails → only test files change → same test passes`

and:

`test command fails → same command passes → no corresponding file edit`

These can indicate that an agent changed a test instead of fixing the underlying issue.

Rashomon currently runs as a Claude Code plugin or through the CLI.

CLI:

`rashomon watch`

then:

`rashomon report`

Plugin:

`/rashomon:report`

There are still edge cases around cwd, git state, test-selection arguments, generated files, retries, and parallel execution. I would be interested in feedback from people building agents on what execution signals you would want Rashomon to capture or correlate.

GitHub: https://github.com/altrace-dev-role/rashomon
